## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Samuddajātaka* (Ja 296), titled "Drinking Sea Water" in English, is a verse narrative from the Pali Jātaka collection [SuttaCentral]. According to the frame narrative (*paccuppannavatthu*), the Buddha delivered the teaching while residing at Jetavana regarding the Elder Upananda, whose greed was insatiable despite cartloads of provisions [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1879]. In the story of the past (*atītavatthu*), set in Bārāṇasī during the reign of King Brahmadatta, the Bodhisatta is reborn as an ocean spirit (*samuddadevatā*) [Fausböll 1879]. The spirit watches a water crow (*udakakāko*) flying over the ocean and strictly warning schools of fish and flocks of birds to drink the sea water only in measured quantities to avoid depleting it [Fausböll 1879]. Witnessing this folly, the sea deity speaks the opening verse (*Ko n' ayam loṇatoyasmiṁ...*), prompting a response from the bird [Fausböll 1879]. The Jātaka is also noted in biographical studies of the Buddha's disciples in connection with an episode where a lay disciple honors the Dhamma by presenting valuable cloth to Ānanda, who offers it to Sāriputta, who gives it to the Buddha [Nyanaponika et al. 2003].

No early cross-language parallels in Chinese, Tibetan, or Sanskrit corpora are recorded for this text [SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus]. DharmaNexus identifies Pali-internal text reuse between the canonical verses and the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* (*Dutiyo bhāgo*), matching four passages with the longest segment alignment running from §1.1–2.4 to §2895–2901 of the commentary [DharmaNexus]. SuttaCentral records four modern translations across four languages [SuttaCentral].
